web_evidence.title: James A. Michener: A Critical Companion
web_evidence.note: The scholarly critical study describes Vernor as a frame narrator, documents his personal first-person reports and commentaries after historical sections, and explains that he becomes a participant in the final chapter; the intervening historical narratives center externally narrated characters.

web_evidence.title: Centennial, Chapter 4 scanned text
web_evidence.note: The sustained 'Many Coups of Lame Beaver' excerpt narrates Lame Beaver and other characters externally in third person while using capitalized 'Our People' as the Arapaho self-name.

web_evidence.title: James A. Michener Writing Styles in Centennial
web_evidence.note: The study guide explicitly characterizes the expansive historical story as third-person omniscient, corroborating the dominant person of the historical chapters, though it does not adequately account for Vernor’s first-person frame material.

web_evidence.title: Centenary now: Modernism, James Michener and the crisis of the endless 1970s
web_evidence.note: The extended critical essay identifies Lewis Vernor as the novel’s frame-story narrator and explains that Vernor enters the action in the final chapter, alongside the novel’s long historical narrative stretches.

web_evidence.title: Centennial (novel)
web_evidence.note: Useful structural discovery: it describes fourteen chapters, the book-as-Vernor’s-reports device, recurring editorial cautions, and present-day first and final chapters, but as a synopsis it is not decisive evidence.

person_note: Centennial deliberately combines persons. Lewis Vernor is a participating first-person frame narrator and the putative author of personal reports and cautions; q01958 directly exposes that voice through 'he told me.' The large historical episodes are sustained third-person narratives, independently demonstrated by several Goodreads passages and the chapter-four web excerpt. The capitalized phrase 'Our People' belongs to the Arapaho-centered idiom of an otherwise externally narrated section, while other first-person forms in the sample are dialogue, aphorism, or verse. Because substantial first-person frame/report material surrounds and recurs among substantial third-person historical sections, ALTERNATING is more accurate than the simplified whole-book THIRD descriptions. No credible evidence of sustained second-person narration was found.
